raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's Labor Insurance Act rules on who can receive survivor allowances after an insured worker dies are unconstitutional. The court did not strike the rules down but said Article 27 and Articles 63 to 65 must be revised within two years. Survivors' eligibility should rest on whether they were actually supported by the worker and cannot support themselves.
raw.held: Article 27 and Articles 63 to 65 of the Labor Insurance Act must be amended within two years of the announcement of the interpretation. The revision should follow the court's reasoning and comprehensively review survivor allowances and related matters, taking into account international labor conventions and social security systems such as pensions.

points.text: Labor insurance is a social security measure that the state set up to carry out constitutional policies protecting workers and providing social insurance.
The insurance fund comes from premiums, government subsidies and employer contributions, so it is not the insured person's private property.
Survivor allowances replace lost income so survivors are not left without support. They differ from an inheritable estate, and the eligible survivors are not the same as heirs under the Civil Code.

The six-month rule for adopted children partly aims to prevent fraudulent claims. But the state's constitutional duty to help people unable to live on their own favors a test of actual support by the insured and the child's inability to earn a living.

Spouses, children, parents and grandparents can receive allowances based on family ties, while grandchildren and siblings must show they were supported solely by the insured. The allowance was meant to cover the living costs of people the insured supported, so every claim should require that support and inability to work.

who: Grandchildren and siblings of insured workers

raw.answer: After a strong earthquake in September 1999, the President issued an emergency order and the Executive Yuan issued implementing guidelines, which it sent to the Legislative Yuan. Legislators asked whether those guidelines were constitutional and whether the Legislative Yuan could review them. The court said an emergency order should in principle be complete enough to be carried out without further supplementary rules. If supplementary rules are needed, the order must say so, and the rules must be issued after the Legislative Yuan ratifies the order and then be sent to it for review. The guidelines did not follow this procedure, but the court found no constitutional violation.
raw.held: Emergency orders should in principle not authorize supplementary rules. Where needed, the order must expressly say so, the rules are issued only after ratification, and they must be submitted to the Legislative Yuan for review and lapse when the order expires. The 1999 guidelines did not match this but were not unconstitutional.

points.text: An emergency order is a stopgap measure made directly under the Constitution's additional articles. It can temporarily replace or change statutes, and it is an exception to the normal division between lawmaking and executing the law, so its content should be thorough enough to be carried out without supplementary rules.

If haste prevents spelling out detailed or technical matters, the order must expressly state that supplementary rules will follow, and the executing agency issues them only after the Legislative Yuan has ratified the order.
Such supplementary rules, whatever they are called, must be sent to the Legislative Yuan under the review procedure for administrative orders.
The Legislative Yuan's ratification is a democratic check. It may only approve or reject the order, not change it, but it may ratify part of it.
Supplementary rules lapse when the emergency order expires, and the order loses effect to the extent the Legislative Yuan passes laws replacing its content.

Before this ruling, the law was unclear on whether agencies could make supplementary rules and whether they had to be sent for review, so the 1999 guidelines, though not matching this ruling, were not unconstitutional.

who: The President and the Executive Yuan
The Legislative Yuan and its members

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance letter was unconstitutional. The letter required companies seeking investment incentives for expanded equipment to finish their capital-increase registration before the new equipment began operating or providing services. The court found that this requirement added a restriction not found in the law or its implementing rules, conflicted with the constitutional principle that restrictions on rights need a legal basis, and should not be applied.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance's 1975 letter, which required the capital-increase registration to be completed before the new equipment began operating, conflicts with the implementing rules and with Article 23 of the Constitution. It must not be applied.

points.text: Under the Act, a qualifying producer that expands equipment by increasing capital may choose one of the listed incentives.

The implementing rules say that a company choosing a four-year income tax exemption must apply to the Ministry of Finance within one year after the new equipment starts operating or providing services. They do not require registration first.

Under the Company Act, after shareholders approve a capital increase and new shares are issued, the company may use the money paid in. Registration of the change is a separate step, finalized when the authority issues a new license.
Using the new equipment to operate or provide services is not forbidden by law, so completing the registration is not a precondition for starting operation.

The letter therefore conflicts with the implementing rules. As an interpretive administrative rule, it added a restriction on rights the law gives people, contrary to the legal-basis principle in Article 23 of the Constitution.

who: Companies seeking investment incentives for expanded equipment
Ministry of Finance and tax authorities

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's irrigation association organization rules, which say who pays water-handling fees and small channel upkeep costs, are unconstitutional. The court held they are not, because the rules only confirm a long-standing custom. It said the fees among small irrigation group members are private-law matters, so disputes go to civil court.
raw.held: The relevant provisions of the irrigation association rules do not conflict with the constitutional protection of property. Fees and upkeep costs among small group members follow private-law principles, and disputes over them go through civil litigation.

points.text: Irrigation associations are public-law legal persons whose members are by law the landholders and beneficiaries in their area. They are comparable to local self-governing bodies and have self-rule within what the law authorizes.

The rules on members' rights and duties and on the association's organization and staffing serve the public interest and fit the law's authorization, so they do not conflict with constitutional property protection or the limits on restricting rights.

By long custom, small irrigation groups manage water distribution and channel upkeep themselves, by labor or money, and the members decide the amounts. So the fees among group members follow private-law principles, and disputes go to civil court.

This differs from the fees, construction costs and usage charges the association collects from members, which are public-law burdens. That the association may collect the fees on behalf of groups, or subsidize them, does not change their nature.
The rule provisions making members bear the fees and upkeep costs only confirm that custom and do not alter its nature, so they do not conflict with property protection.

The court noted that, since the association is a public-law body and administrative litigation has been reformed, it should be reviewed whether to keep the private-law custom or make these fees public-law burdens set by statute. It also said a regional group-meeting guideline is not a law or order and cannot be reviewed.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a 1996 Administrative Court resolution was constitutional. It said an expropriation stays valid even if the compensation was not paid within the legal time limit. The court decided that this view conflicts with the constitutional protection of property, so it must not be applied.
raw.held: Compensation for expropriated property must be reasonable and paid promptly. If the compensation is not paid within 15 days, or within a reasonable period in special cases, the expropriation approval loses effect. The Administrative Court's contrary resolution is not to be applied.

points.text: Article 15 of the Constitution protects property rights, so the state may expropriate property for public use or other public interest only with reasonable compensation.
Compensation is a special sacrifice made for the public interest, so it must cover the owner's loss. It must be adequate and also paid as quickly as possible.

Article 233 of the Land Act requires compensation within 15 days after the public notice ends. Even when an objection delays this, the amount must be passed on within the same 15-day limit once it is assessed.

The strict procedure aims to protect people's property while the state serves the public interest. If the owner refuses payment and the money is deposited, extra compensation ordered later that goes unpaid means the expropriation cannot be treated as unaffected.
Expropriation and compensation are inseparable. Article 235 of the Land Act ends the owner's rights only when compensation has been fully paid.

If the extra amount is very large or there are special circumstances, payment must still be made promptly within a reasonable period after the assessment is final. Otherwise the expropriation approval loses effect.

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 25 of the Physicians Act, as amended in 1986, is unconstitutional. It let authorities suspend a doctor for one month to one year, or revoke the license, for illegal or improper conduct in practice. The court held that the rule is not unconstitutional because it is clear enough and is a necessary measure.
raw.held: The 1986 Article 25 of the Physicians Act does not violate the principle of legal clarity, does not conflict with the constitutional protection of people's rights, and is consistent with Article 23 of the Constitution.

points.text: Professional discipline rules may use open-ended terms, because life is complex. They are acceptable if their meaning is understandable, people can foresee what breaches duty and what punishment follows, and courts can review them.

'Illegal conduct in practice' means conduct in medical work that, by professional knowledge, is objectively understood as not permitted by law. It is limited to medical-practice acts and does not cover every illegal act by a doctor, so its scope can be determined.

'Improper conduct in practice' means medical conduct that falls short of illegality but goes against medical theory and medical ethics and lacks legitimacy. Such conduct cannot be listed in full detail, so open-ended concepts are used.
In individual cases, a properly composed body can decide the meaning using professional knowledge and common social understanding, and courts can review it. So the rule meets the clarity principle.
Illegal or improper conduct by doctors endangers medical safety and public health, and improper fee claims can erode the finances of national health insurance.
Letting the authority choose a penalty by the degree of harm is necessary to uphold medical ethics, keep social order and promote the public interest, so it does not conflict with Article 23.

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 31 of the National Health Insurance Act and the medical rules issued under it are unconstitutional. The court found that Article 31 is too broad and unclear, and that the 1995 medical measures and related internal guidelines went beyond what the law allowed. It ordered the problem parts of the law and the related orders to be reviewed and corrected within two years.
raw.held: Article 31 of the Act violates the principle of legal clarity, and the 1995 medical measures exceeded the law's authorization. The problem parts of the law and related orders must be reviewed and corrected within two years of the ruling's announcement.

points.text: National health insurance is compulsory social insurance affecting everyone, so rights and duties under it need clear rules and must rest on law. Any authorization to fill in details by order must be specific, clear and foreseeable to the insured.

When the law lets the agency issue regulations through a set procedure, it must use them and cannot replace them with internal administrative rules. Without authority to sub-delegate, it cannot hand rule-making to its subordinate bodies.

Article 39 is meant to define clearly what is not covered. For the catch-all item 12, the agency must announce non-covered services and drugs in advance and cannot issue other exclusions instead; if that is not enough, the law can be amended.
Article 31 is too broad and unclear. The medical measures under it should concern outpatient or inpatient care only.

The 1995 measures unilaterally changed the insured's basic rights and duties, and Article 31(2) passed the setting of high-tech items and review procedures to the insurer without authority, exceeding the law.

Article 41(3) on prior review sets no items or standards for refusing payment and requires prior review regardless of urgent need, which conflicts with protecting the insured. The payment-standard and drug-price provisions cannot be used to define what is excluded from coverage.

Excluding coverage through broadly delegated regulations is already inadequate, and replacing them with internal administrative guidelines not clearly authorized by law violates the legal reservation principle.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a court-practice rule is unconstitutional. The rule says that when property under provisional seizure or a provisional injunction is compulsorily purchased or expropriated by the government, the enforcement court must deposit the price or compensation with the court. The Constitutional Court held that the rule is not unconstitutional.
raw.held: The rule (point 70 of the enforcement notes) requiring the court to deposit the purchase price or compensation does not conflict with Article 5 of the Central Regulations Standards Act, and it does not violate the constitutional protection of property rights.

points.text: Provisional measures that stop a debtor from transferring property are a preliminary enforcement step. They secure the creditor's eventual claim and are needed to maintain social order and advance the public interest.

Seized property cannot block a government purchase or expropriation, but the price or compensation stands in for the property. The ban on transfer therefore continues to cover that money, and a provisional injunction turns into a provisional seizure.
The deposit rule only declares that the original seizure's effect continues over the substitute. This preserves the creditor's future claim.
Depositing the money does not extinguish the debt, and it adds no restriction on the debtor's rights and leaves the debtor no worse off.

The rule is consistent with the cited Compulsory Enforcement Act provisions, so it does not conflict with Article 5 of the Central Regulations Standards Act or with the constitutional protection of property.
If the substitute can no longer achieve the purpose of securing the claim, whether the debtor may object under the Enforcement Act is a separate question.

who: Debtors whose property is under provisional seizure or a provisional injunction
Creditors seeking to secure future claims
Government bodies that purchase or expropriate property

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Act for Upgrading Industries could constitutionally let the authorities force a buyback of industrial-zone land or factory buildings that a business did not use as planned. The court held that the forced buyback itself is constitutional. But it held that if the buyback happens for reasons not attributable to the business, refusing to return the development fund payment already collected is contrary to the Constitution's protection of people's rights.
raw.held: The forced-buyback rule (Article 38) fits the proportionality principle and does not violate property rights. The implementing rule that excludes the paid fund money from the buyback price is unconstitutional if it blocks a refund where the business was not at fault.

points.text: The buyback rule aims to make sure industrial-zone land and factories are used promptly for industrial upgrading and economic development, and to stop buyers from using state-developed zones and tax incentives to resell for profit or use the property for other purposes.

Because of this aim, forced buyback is necessary for the public interest, meets the proportionality principle in Article 23 of the Constitution, and does not conflict with property protection. The authority may buy back whatever the reason for non-use or non-compliant use.

The development and management fund is charged only to those who buy zone land or buildings and is used for zone development and management. It works like a special levy and usage fee on a group with a shared interest, and is not part of the purchase price.
Leaving the fund out of the buyback price is acceptable for buyers who paid but failed to use the property within the year.

If the buyback is for reasons not attributable to the business, it was never a member of the levied group and has no usage relationship. The basis and purpose of the charge disappear, and a business that later buys in another zone would be charged again.

The fund payment then becomes an unjust enrichment in public law, so the business may bring a payment suit. The implementing rule is unconstitutional if it denies a refund, but does not bar that claim. Whether the business was at fault or got other compensation is a factual matter left outside this ruling.

who: Businesses that bought or leased industrial-zone land or factories
Industrial authorities that carry out buybacks
Businesses bought back through no fault of their own

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule letting a court order a person to be held ("留置") before a decision on a hoodlum-related 感訓 measure is unconstitutional. The court found that Article 11, paragraph 1 of the 檢肅流氓條例 went beyond what is necessary, because it did not clearly say when a court may order the holding. That part of the rule will lose effect one year after the ruling is announced.
raw.held: Article 11(1) of the 檢肅流氓條例, to the extent that it leaves the conditions for ordering a holding to the court's own discretion, is inconsistent with Articles 8 and 23 of the Constitution and loses effect one year after the ruling is announced. Until the law is properly amended, courts must weigh holding orders carefully in line with this ruling.

points.text: Any measure restricting personal freedom, whether or not the person is a criminal defendant, must follow a procedure set by law, be substantively fair, and meet the conditions of Article 23 of the Constitution.
The holding is meant to keep the later proceedings on track, but it is a serious restriction on personal freedom because it confines the person to a set place before the measure is finalized.
The holding resembles detention (羈押) in criminal procedure in purpose, but the statute deliberately uses a different name and different conditions, so the two cannot be treated as the same.
Giving courts broad discretion over holding may be necessary to protect social order, but rules that limit people's rights must still be clear and respect basic-rights protection and proportionality.

The statute does not clearly state when a court may order a holding. Apart from cases of direct arrest under Articles 6 and 7, where the court has already confirmed grounds for arrest, it leaves the decision to the court even when there is no risk of continued serious disruption of order or of flight, destroying evidence, or threatening witnesses.
For that reason the provision goes beyond what is necessary, conflicts with Articles 8 and 23, and loses effect in one year, with courts to weigh holding orders carefully in the meantime.

who: People referred to a court for a 感訓 ruling

raw.answer: The case asked whether a provision of the Customs Anti-Smuggling Act that broadly punishes false declarations of an imported good's country of origin is unconstitutional. The court decided it is not, within the stated scope, because the punishment is needed to enforce customs and trade-control rules. It also said punishment still requires intent or negligence.
raw.held: Article 37, paragraph 1, item 4 of the Customs Anti-Smuggling Act is read to cover goods imported in violation of the law in ways similar to the false declarations in the first three items. Punishing false declaration of origin within that scope does not conflict with Article 23 of the Constitution, and punishment under Articles 36 and 37 still requires intent or negligence.

points.text: Clarity of law does not require detailed wording; lawmakers may use general clauses given the complexity of life, as long as the meaning is understandable, foreseeable and reviewable by courts.

The general clause on 'other illegal acts' is meant to punish importing goods in violation of the law in ways similar to the false declarations in the first three items, in order to ensure honest declarations.
Customs, trade and cross-strait laws let the government control or restrict trade with particular countries or regions for national security and orderly trade.

Enforcing those rules depends on knowing a good's origin, so false origin declarations would undermine trade-control policy; punishing them is necessary and fits the Act's purpose, so it does not violate Article 23.
Punishment under Articles 36 and 37 still requires the person's intent or negligence, as Interpretation No. 275 applies.

who: Persons who declare goods' origin to customs

raw.answer: The case asked whether guidelines issued by Taiwan's Fair Trade Commission, on when sending warning letters about alleged infringement of copyright, trademark or patent rights counts as a legitimate use of rights, are unconstitutional. The court decided they are not unconstitutional. It found they only interpret the law, and do not add new limits on people's rights.
raw.held: The Fair Trade Commission's guidelines (points 3 and 4) on warning letters about infringement of intellectual property rights do not conflict with the Constitution. They do not add legal restrictions, so they do not violate the principle of legal reservation or raise any question of clear authorization.

points.text: An agency may issue necessary interpretive rules to carry out the law it enforces, and these serve as the basis for its officials' work.
Because market conduct keeps changing, the legislature uses open-ended legal concepts, and the agency may interpret them through administrative rules.

Article 45 of the Fair Trade Act balances protecting intellectual property owners against keeping competition free and fair, so the agency must weigh both interests when deciding what is a legitimate exercise of rights.

The guidelines treat a warning letter as legitimate if it has a first-instance court judgment or an impartial expert report and prior notice, or if it clearly states the rights and the specific infringement and breaks no prohibition. This is a reasonable reading of an open-ended concept.

The ban on abusing rights is a basic principle of law, so the duty not to abuse a patent right was not added by the guidelines. Sending vague warning letters to competitors' customers to hurt competition is not a legitimate use of patent rights and falls under the Fair Trade Act.
The guidelines are only illustrative interpretations that add no limits on rights beyond the law, so they do not violate legal reservation and raise no authorization problem.

who: Businesses and customers receiving such letters

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance letter of 1990 was unconstitutional. The letter said that when tax officials work out the net asset value of an unlisted company for inheritance or gift tax, the listed-company shares it holds must be valued at their closing price. The court held that the letter does not conflict with the Constitution, but added that the method for valuing unlisted company shares should be set by law or by rules authorized by law.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance letter of 6 September 1990 is consistent with the legislative intent of Article 10(1) of the Estate and Gift Tax Act and does not conflict with the constitutional principle of taxation by law (Art. 19) or the protection of property rights (Art. 15). The court added that methods for valuing unlisted or non-OTC company shares affect tax burdens and should be set by law or under a legal authorization in the enforcement rules.

points.text: The Act values estate and gift property at its market price at the time of death or gift, and the enforcement rules set closing prices for listed shares and net asset value for unlisted company shares.
Unlisted shares often have no trades, or only non-public trades, so their objective market value is hard to determine. That is why net asset value is used.
Listed shares held by an unlisted company are traded on a public market, so they may be adjusted to closing prices before the company's net asset value is calculated.
Using the company's book cost would give different values for the same listed shares depending on purchase timing, which would violate fair taxation.
The letter only clarifies what the enforcement rules mean and fits the Act's intent, so it does not conflict with Articles 19 and 15 of the Constitution.

The applicant argued the letter, issued in September, was applied retroactively to events in April and August 1990. The court said an official interpretation that clarifies the original meaning of a rule applies from the rule's effective date (Interpretation No. 287), so no constitutional problem arises.

who: Heirs and donees taxed on estates or gifts
Unlisted or non-OTC companies holding listed shares

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's traffic-fine rules, which set a minimum fine and fixed fine amounts, are unconstitutional. The court held that the detailed rules it reviewed stay within what the parent law allows and do not conflict with the constitutional protection of property rights. It also said courts can still change a fine if they find the original decision unlawful or inappropriate.
raw.held: The traffic-fine rules examined (paying the minimum fine voluntarily, and fixed fine amounts for late or non-appearing offenders) do not go beyond the law's authorization, do not violate the legal reservation principle, and do not conflict with property rights. A court hearing an objection may still change a penalty if the original decision was unlawful or inappropriate.

points.text: The law lets a person who accepts the reported violation pay the lowest fine for that provision voluntarily within fifteen days. The detailed rules (Articles 41(1) and 48(1)) only spell out this idea, so they do not exceed the parent law's authorization or the legal reservation principle.

This differs from Interpretation No. 423, which involved vehicle air-pollution fines set without authorization from the air pollution law. Pollution varies by source and amount, so basing fines only on arrival time would not fit the authorization's purpose, whereas traffic violations are defined simply by breaking traffic rules.
Fixed fine amounts for people who miss the payment deadline or are fined without appearing are discretion guidelines the law lets the authority set.
The fine amounts do not exceed the legal upper limit. They also encourage voluntary payment, avoid later enforcement trouble and save administrative cost.
Fixed amounts help prevent different agencies from imposing arbitrarily different fines for the same case, so they are not forbidden by law and do not conflict with property rights.
A person who disagrees with a fine can object in court. If the court finds the decision unlawful or inappropriate, it may change the penalty even if the person missed the date or sent someone else.

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's road traffic penalty rules are unconstitutional when they revoke the licence of a driver who flees after a crash that injures or kills someone, and then bar that driver from taking the licence test again. The court decided both rules do not conflict with Article 23 of the Constitution. It also asked the authorities to review quickly whether people who have shown they can readjust or improve should get a chance to re-apply after certain conditions or a number of years.
raw.held: The licence revocation for fleeing after an injury or fatal crash, and the bar on re-taking the licence test, are not unconstitutional under Article 23. The relevant authorities should promptly review whether a driver who has shown real improvement should be allowed to re-apply under certain conditions or after a set period.

points.text: After a crash with injury or death, drivers must give aid or take necessary steps right away to stop the harm from spreading, and fleeing makes fault hard to determine and may leave victims without help or compensation, so strict treatment is justified.
Revoking the licence of a driver who flees aims to improve road safety, protect others' rights and maintain social order, so it does not conflict with Article 23.
The ban on re-taking the licence test is a needed public policy to protect crash victims' lives and health.
The ban also requires drivers to take up their social responsibility for road safety, which serves social order and the public interest, so it is not contrary to Article 23.

Still, where a person whose licence was revoked shows concrete signs of readjusting to society or improving, authorities should consider offering a chance to re-apply under conditions or after a period, to better fit the Constitution's protection of people's rights.

who: Drivers who flee after a crash causing injury or death

raw.answer: A taxpayer who had been through a business tax case asked the court to clarify its earlier Interpretation No. 356, which did not say whether a penalty for failing to carry out a required duty and a penalty for tax evasion must both be imposed. The court said that when one act meets the conditions for both penalties, the person generally cannot be punished twice. Two penalties are allowed only where they are different in kind and both are needed to achieve the government's purpose.
raw.held: If one act meets the conditions for both a penalty for breaching a duty and a penalty for tax evasion, the person may not be punished twice, unless the penalties differ in nature and kind and both are needed for the administrative purpose. Where the breach is part of, or a means of, the evasion and the penalties are of the same kind, only the heavier one applies if that is enough. Interpretation No. 356 is supplemented accordingly.

points.text: The court accepted the request because the final court judgment relied on Interpretation No. 356, which did not say whether the two penalties are combined or only the heavier one applies.
The two penalties differ in purpose and conditions: one applies to any breach of a duty, the other only where the legally defined tax-evasion facts exist.

Even so, not punishing the same conduct twice is a basic principle of modern democratic states under the rule of law, except where the penalties differ in nature and kind (for example a fine and a confiscation, or a fine and a business suspension) and both are needed for the administrative purpose.

If the breach is part of the evasion or a means of it and the penalties are of the same kind, imposing the heavier one is enough when it achieves the administrative purpose, and no further penalty may be added, in keeping with the constitutional protection of people's rights.
Interpretation No. 356 only distinguished the two penalties by nature; it did not mean both must always be imposed together, so each case must apply this reasoning.

who: Businesses that fail to issue required receipts

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Police Duty Ordinance's provisions allowing police to carry out stop-and-check operations (臨檢) are unconstitutional. The court found that the provision is not unconstitutional in itself, but it may be applied only within strict limits that protect people's freedom, property and privacy. It also said the rules on police duties are incomplete and must be reviewed within two years.
raw.held: The ordinance's provision on stop-and-check operations (Article 11, item 3) may be applied only within the limits the court set out, such as a reasonable basis for checking, proportionality, and stating the reason and showing identification. The relevant authorities must review and complete the rules within two years of the ruling's publication.

points.text: The petitioner could challenge the ordinance because the criminal judgment depended on whether the officer was lawfully performing duties under it.
The ordinance sets out police duty teams and methods, so it is more than an organizational law and also works as a law regulating conduct. Stop-and-check is one of the listed methods.

Stop-and-check measures (inspection, roadblocks, enforcement, questioning) interfere with people or things and seriously affect freedom of movement, property and privacy. The conditions, procedures and remedies for them therefore need clear legal rules.

The legislature did not intend to let police stop and check anyone at will regardless of time, place or person. Place checks are limited to places where harm has occurred or is reasonably judged likely, and checks on persons require reasonable grounds to believe harm has occurred or is about to occur. All checks must be proportionate.

Police must state the reason and show identification before a check. The check should happen on the spot, and people may be taken to the station only in limited cases. Once identity is established, the person must be allowed to leave.

Unlawful checks must be open to remedies. Until the law is completed, people may object during the check, and a written record of the check, which counts as an administrative disposition, can be challenged. The rules governing police duties are also incomplete and must be reviewed within two years.

who: People stopped or checked by police
Owners and users of places and vehicles checked
Authorities responsible for revising police duty rules

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the Chinese medicine practitioner screening measures was unconstitutional. The rule required overseas Chinese who held special "僑" certificates to take a written exam when they returned to practise. The court decided the rule does not violate the Constitution.
raw.held: The rule requiring holders of the "僑" Chinese medicine certificates to sit a written exam on returning to practise is not unconstitutional. It does not breach the principle of clear delegation of authority, equality, or protection of reasonable reliance.

points.text: The Constitution requires professional qualifications to be set through examinations by the Examination Yuan. Doctors need specialist knowledge because their work affects public health.

The Physicians Act set the main requirements and delegated technical details, such as the screening subjects and methods, to the Examination Yuan and the Executive Yuan. This delegation was clear enough.

Changing the make-up exam from a "face test" to a written exam was only a change in examination technique within the delegated authority. It did not affect the certificates already issued, and it added no limit beyond the parent law.

The rule does not violate equality. Equality means substantive equality, and certificate holders who skipped the exam cannot claim the same right to practise domestically as those who passed it. Otherwise the exam could be avoided.
The term "face test" never meant only an oral exam. It included written exams, and all of these are ways of selecting talent.

Holders of the "僑中" certificate had no qualification to practise at home, so they had no reliance interest to protect. The measures took effect without a transition period, and the court found no breach of reliance protection. The later Physicians Act transition rule did not affect rights already acquired.

who: Overseas Chinese holding 僑 or 僑中 Chinese medicine certificates
Chinese medicine practitioners seeking to practise in Taiwan
Candidates who passed the domestic screening exam

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's highest judicial body may make rules about how cases are handled, and how far its supervisory orders may go. The court held that it may make rules on technical and procedural details and may issue supervisory orders, as long as these do not undermine judges' independence in deciding cases or conflict with the law. It also said the Judicial Yuan's structure should be reviewed and amended within two years.
raw.held: The highest judicial body may issue rules on technical, detailed trial procedure and supervisory orders, but these must not violate judicial independence, conflict with statutes, or add limits on people's rights without a clear legal authorization. The laws on the Judicial Yuan and the courts must be reviewed and amended within two years of the ruling.

points.text: Article 80 of the Constitution protects judges' independence: they are bound only by law, and their position is not affected by their rulings. This is an important principle of separation and balance of powers.
To make judicial independence real, the judiciary needs autonomy, including the power to make rules on technical and detailed matters of trial procedure so that proceedings are fair and quick.

To protect people's right to fair and effective trials, the highest judicial body has administrative supervision power over judges, including checking diligence, asking for explanations of delays, and handling other administrative matters, as long as the core of judging is untouched.
Supervisory orders must not conflict with the law or add limits on people's rights without clear legal authorization. Legal views in them do not bind judges when deciding cases.

Prosecutors work under the principle of prosecutorial unity and are directed by their chief prosecutors, which differs from judicial independence. The Minister of Justice may issue supervisory orders on prosecution administration.

The Judicial Yuan is the highest judicial organ under the Constitution, but it is now mainly an administrative body separated from top adjudication. The related organization laws must be reviewed and amended within two years.

who: Judicial Yuan and Ministry of Justice

raw.answer: The case asked which court process applies when a medical facility and the Bureau of National Health Insurance disagree over their contract. The court decided the contract is an administrative contract, so such disputes are public-law matters. After the review procedure under the National Health Insurance Act, a facility that is still dissatisfied may bring an administrative lawsuit.
raw.held: The contract between the Bureau and a medical facility is an administrative contract, and disputes over it are public-law disputes that go through administrative litigation. A facility unhappy with the review result may bring an administrative action as the law allows.

points.text: The right to sue protects people whose rights are harmed. The legislature decides whether a case goes to ordinary or administrative courts, and Taiwan has two separate court systems: ordinary courts for private-law disputes and administrative courts for public-law disputes.
The Bureau is a state body carrying out national health insurance, which is compulsory social insurance of a public-law nature.

The contract's main content is that facilities treat insured people and the Bureau pays the approved fees. The payment aims to make facilities follow public-law rules and so serve public health and the public interest.
The Bureau can give guidance and fine facilities, which gives it a superior position, so the contract is an administrative contract and disputes over it are public-law disputes.
The Administrative Litigation Act allows public-law disputes, including payments arising from public-law contracts, to be brought as administrative lawsuits, and this system is well developed.

The Act did not say what route facilities should take after a review decision, and the Bureau's contracts named an ordinary court. The court said this was not objectionable before, but after the new administrative litigation system began, such disputes should go through administrative procedures.

who: Medical service institutions contracted with national health insurance

raw.answer: The case was about a 1994 Taiwan Province government set of review rules that let certain industrial (kiln) building land in hillside conservation, scenic and forest zones be changed to non-industrial use if it met two conditions. The court found the rules went beyond the parent law, created new conditions for changing land-use designations, and added limits on people's use of their land. It therefore held the rules contrary to the constitutional requirement that such limits rest on law, and they are not to be applied.
raw.held: The court held that sections 2 and 3 of the review rules exceed the scope of the parent law, add restrictions on people's land rights, and conflict with the legal-reservation principle in Article 23 of the Constitution, so they are not to be applied.

points.text: Land is essential to people's lives, and the Regional Planning Act was made to balance different land uses against the public interest; non-urban land is controlled by zoning and designated uses, with rules set by the central authority under delegation.

The review rules, though they cite the land-use control rules as their basis, are in substance only supplementary rules by the provincial government, so they may cover only minor, detailed and technical matters of carrying out the parent law.

Under the Regional Planning Act and the control rules, non-urban land must be zoned and controlled, used only as its designation allows, and changed only through set procedures such as periodic reviews or an approved business plan.

Sections 2 and 3 of the review rules set their own conditions for changing land designations (government-led relocation from reservoir or water-protection areas, or public facility or government use), which the parent law and control rules do not provide.

This goes against the purpose of zoning and controlling non-urban land and adds limits on people's rights to use their land, so it is not a mere detailed rule and violates the legal-reservation principle in Article 23.

who: Owners of kiln-type industrial building land
Landowners in hillside conservation, scenic and forest zones

raw.answer: The case asked whether a patent law rule requiring a patent holder to attach an infringement appraisal report before filing a criminal complaint is constitutional. The court decided the rule places an unnecessary limit on people's right to bring legal action and breaks the proportionality principle. The requirement and its consequence are no longer to be applied from the date of the ruling.
raw.held: The patent law provisions requiring an infringement appraisal report to be attached to a complaint (Article 131, paragraph 2), and making a complaint without it invalid (paragraph 3), are not to be applied from the date the interpretation is published.

points.text: The constitutional right to bring legal action covers seeking redress from judicial bodies, including criminal justice, and the state must provide institutional protection for it. Laws may reasonably limit how it is used, but only within the proportionality principle of Article 23.
Under criminal procedure, expert appraisal is a kind of evidence that applies only after proceedings begin, and the prosecutor or court chooses the appraiser.
Even if the victim submits an appraisal report, prosecutors or courts must still investigate the evidence themselves and cannot decide a crime occurred on the report alone.
Making the report a condition for filing a complaint is therefore an unnecessary limit on the right to sue and violates the proportionality principle.
Appraisal bodies might refuse requests, delay, or be unable to handle fast-changing patent content, so patent holders could miss the legal deadline to file a complaint.
A patent holder who files a written complaint that specifically points to evidence of infringement has made a valid complaint.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the Land Act limiting the right of former owners to buy back expropriated land is unconstitutional when the land went unused because of someone other than the government. The court held that the rule is not unconstitutional as long as it is applied in line with the ruling's reading. Under that reading, former owners can still reclaim land where the delay was not their fault and the authorities and the user of the land did not act.
raw.held: Article 219, paragraph 3 of the Land Act does not conflict with the Constitution when applied within the ruling's meaning. If the delay in using the land is not attributable to the former owner and the authorities and the land-using body failed to act within the period, the former owner's reclaim right is not blocked.

points.text: Land ownership is protected and limited by law, and expropriation must meet the necessity principle in Article 23 of the Constitution.
The reclaim right exists to prevent unnecessary expropriation, poorly prepared plans, or delay by the body that needs the land, so it is kept for the former owner.
If the delay in using the land is the fault of the former owner or of users occupying the land for the owner, the delay cannot be blamed on the expropriating side.

If the delay is due to other users and not the owner, and the local land authorities did not remove or move the improvements within one year and the land-needing body also did not bring necessary lawsuits, the owner should not be blocked from reclaiming.
Denying reclaim in that situation would put the disadvantage on the former owner even though the authorities and the land-needing body failed to act.

If the land was already put to use as public property before this ruling and reclaiming would seriously harm the public interest, the owner cannot reclaim it but may seek compensation based on the expropriation price at the time of use.

who: Bodies needing land for public projects

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance directive taxing golf course membership fees and deposits was unconstitutional. The directive says clubs must issue invoices and pay business tax (and entertainment tax) when they collect these amounts, with a refund of the tax if a member later leaves and gets the money back. The court found the directive did not go beyond the Business Tax Act and did not violate the Constitution.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance directive is consistent with the Business Tax Act's scope, fits the principle of fair taxation, and does not conflict with the Constitution's equality right (Article 7) or its principle of taxation by law (Article 19).

points.text: The Business Tax Act applies to sales of goods or services in Taiwan, and a business's taxable sales include all the payment received, including entrance fees or deposits that are in substance payment for goods or services.
Tax laws must be read in line with the principle of taxation by law, their purpose, their economic meaning and fair substance-based taxation, as an earlier interpretation (No. 420) said.
Even if an amount is called a deposit, it is still taxed if it is in reality payment for goods or services.
Taxing first and refunding tax on amounts that truly are deposits when returned is a way to carry out the Act and check taxes, preventing avoidance through relabeling.

Because the directive covers only fees or deposits that are in substance payment for goods or services, it stays within the Act's scope, is fair, and does not conflict with Articles 7 and 19 of the Constitution.

raw.answer: The case concerned Education Ministry rules for amusement arcades that barred electronic game businesses from letting people under 18 enter, and allowed the business's permit to be revoked if they did. The court found that these two provisions limit people's right to work and property without a basis in a statute or a clear statutory authorization. It held them contrary to the Constitution and said they should not be applied.
raw.held: Section 13, item 12 (no entry for under-18s at electronic game businesses) and Section 17, paragraph 3 (permit revocation for breaking that rule) of the arcade management rules violate the legal reservation principle in Article 23 of the Constitution and are not to be applied.

points.text: Freedom to run a business is protected as part of the right to work and property under the Constitution.

Conditions for a business permit, the duties businesses must follow, and penalties for breaking them limit these rights, so under Article 23 they must be set by statute, and any authorization to make orders must be specific and clear in purpose, content and scope.
The ministry issued the rules to protect public order, good morals and the health of children and youths when the legal system was incomplete, which met a real need.

The ban on under-18s entering is a duty on businesses and limits their freedom to choose customers, and revoking the permit is a penalty for breaching that duty, so both need a statute or statutory authorization.

Statutes on youth and child welfare already cover these matters, so the authority should not keep using an order lacking statutory authorization, as the rule of law requires administration according to law.
Someone whose conduct was unlawful under the law at the time cannot claim relief just because the related order was later held not applicable.

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Ministry of the Interior's contractor-management rules were unconstitutional, in particular the rule requiring construction firms in Kinmen and Lienchiang (Matsu) to swap their old wartime-era registration certificates for new ones. The court held that the grading system and the swap rule do not violate the Constitution. It added that major limits on business freedom, such as grading conditions and caps on the size of jobs, would be better set by law or by a regulation clearly authorized by law.
raw.held: The contractor grading rules and the swap-or-be-downgraded rule for Kinmen and Lienchiang firms (Article 45-1) are not unconstitutional and do not go beyond the authority in Building Act Article 15, paragraph 2. The court also said grading conditions and job-size caps should preferably be set by law or by a regulation clearly authorized by law.

points.text: The Building Act lets the Ministry of the Interior make contractor management rules. Although it does not spell out the scope, reading the law as a whole shows the legislature meant to authorize rules on registration, conduct and oversight.

Grading contractors into three classes by capital, professional staff and track record, and capping the jobs each class may take, limits business freedom. But it aims to raise technical standards and protect life, body and property, so it serves the public interest.
After wartime administration ended in Kinmen and Lienchiang on 7 November 1992, the old registration certificates lost their legal basis, so a rule was needed to deal with that change.
Requiring those firms to swap certificates under the national rules supports uniform grading and uniform legal treatment of contractors nationwide, and applies equally to all firms there.
The rule gives a three-year transition period and lets firms swap their certificates, which was not arbitrary or clearly unreasonable and so protects their reliance on the old rules.
Even so, grading conditions and job-size caps heavily restrict business freedom, so they should preferably be set by law or by a regulation clearly authorized by law.

raw.answer: The case was about a plan to relocate residents of three villages in the Feitsui (Jade) Reservoir catchment area to protect water quality and quantity, and about how the plan decided who could receive a relocation payment. The court found the relocation itself consistent with the Constitution's protection of residence and movement. It also found that using household registration as the only proof of residence was not an equality violation but was incomplete, and ordered the rules to be reviewed and improved quickly.
raw.held: The relocation plan does not violate the constitutional freedom of residence and movement, because its means are proportionate to protecting water resources. Making household registration the only test for relocation payments does not breach equality, but it is inadequate because it ignores other proof of residence, so the rules must be reviewed and improved promptly.

points.text: The plan, announced after approval by the Executive Yuan, counts as an administrative order the court can review.
Freedom of residence and movement may be limited only as far as necessary and with a clear legal basis; the Water Supply Act, Article 11, authorizes protected water zones and bans harmful acts there.
The relocation plan aims to protect water quality and quantity, and its means help reach that aim and are objectively necessary, so it meets proportionality and does not violate Article 10.

Administrative orders that grant benefits, such as payments, must follow constitutional principles, especially equality, and such social policy needs a legitimate aim and means that are effective and necessary.
The relocation payment aims to help residents leave the catchment area, so it should depend on actual residence; household registration is only one way to show that.

Using registration as the only standard leaves out people who actually lived there but were not registered, which is incomplete though not an equality violation; those who can otherwise prove long residence before 1 January 1980 should still be paid.

who: Residents of Bishan, Yongan and Getou villages
Residents who lived there without household registration
Administrative agencies running the relocation plan

raw.answer: The Executive Yuan decided to stop building the Fourth Nuclear Power Plant and to stop spending its budget, and a dispute arose with the Legislative Yuan. The court held that stopping a legally approved budget item is not automatically unlawful, but because this change affected an important national policy, the Executive Yuan had to report to the Legislative Yuan and answer questions. The court did not decide whether nuclear power or other energy is better.
raw.held: Stopping a budget item that reflects an important national policy change requires the Premier or relevant ministers to report to the Legislative Yuan and face questioning, and the Executive Yuan must promptly make up this report; the Legislative Yuan must listen to it.

points.text: A passed budget is similar to a law in form but differs in content, who it binds and how it is reviewed. Stopping part of it is not automatically unlawful; where no important policy change is involved and budget law conditions are met, agencies have some flexibility.

That flexibility is limited: funds needed to keep an agency running cannot be stopped if that threatens its existence, and agencies cannot freely choose which approved items to carry out. Budget rules and the budget review (veto) procedure show an approved budget has binding force.

The Legislative Yuan's power to review budgets includes taking part in forming national policy. Because the plant affects energy reserves, environment and industry, is costly and hard to unwind, and both sides agreed it is an important policy, the legislature should have a chance to take part again.

Any change of policy must follow the constitutional order of checks and balances and legal procedure. Under Article 17 of the Legislative Yuan Functions Act, important matters or policy changes require a report and questioning, which was not done here, so the process was flawed.
The legislature's boycott of the report was also not a proper way to protect constitutional operation, so it too must listen to the report.

After the report, if most legislators back the change it can proceed; if the legislature opposes, the bodies should negotiate or use existing constitutional mechanisms, and the court leaves the choice to them.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance letter violated the Constitution by requiring owners to report how a building is used before getting a house tax reduction. The court held that the letter fits the House Tax Act and does not conflict with the constitutional principle that taxes must rest on law. Under it, a factory building owner who had already paid at the business rate before reporting cannot get the half-rate reduction for that earlier period.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance's 1982 letter requires owners whose buildings qualify for a reduction to report the qualifying use with supporting documents. Tax already paid at the business rate before the report cannot be reduced to half. The court held this matches Article 7 of the House Tax Act and does not conflict with the constitutional principle that taxes must rest on law.

points.text: Legally registered factories get half-rate house tax on their own buildings used directly for production, and the Act requires owners to report the building's value and use.

Tax authorities may investigate on their own, but they handle many complex cases, and the facts that decide tax reductions lie within the taxpayer's own sphere, so checking every possible reduction without an application would greatly raise collection costs.
Under the constitutional duty to pay taxes according to law (Article 19), taxpayers have a duty to cooperate by reporting, which is necessary for fair and lawful taxation.

Other tax reduction rules, such as those in the Land Tax Act and the land tax reduction rules, also require the taxpayer to apply, and late applicants get the special rate only from the following year.

The current House Tax Act likewise requires reporting within thirty days, with a late report giving the reduction only from the month of reporting, so reporting is a necessary step for the preferential rate.
The Ministry's letter therefore matches the legislative purpose of these provisions and does not conflict with the constitutional principle that taxes must rest on law.

who: Owners of legally registered factory buildings

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's physical fitness standards for aviation personnel, which can limit or restrict their work, violate the constitution. The court decided they do not. It found the rules were a permitted limit on choosing an occupation, made to protect public safety, and were not a punishment.
raw.held: The Civil Aviation Act's rule that aviation personnel must pass checks, and the Civil Aeronautics Administration's physical standards (Articles 48(1), 52 and 53) that restrict and periodically reassess those with waived defects, do not conflict with the constitutional protection of the right to work.

points.text: The constitution protects the right to work and freedom to choose an occupation. Where a job is closely tied to the public interest, the way of working and the required qualifications may be limited by law, within the proportionality principle in Article 23.
Laws cannot cover every detail, so authorities may be authorized by order to set suitable standards for the knowledge, ability, age and physical fitness that people in a particular occupation need.

Aviation is an important means of transport, aircraft are complex and highly specialized, and they fly fast at altitude, so their safety is closely tied to the public interest. Aviation personnel therefore need professional training, sound body and mind, and adequate physical fitness.

The Civil Aviation Act requires periodic and temporary checks of skill, physical condition and conduct, requires restricting, suspending or ending practice when standards are not met, and authorizes the aviation authority to set the standards.

Under the authority's standards, someone who fails the physical standard is failed, but may have the defect waived after special evaluation if experience means flight safety is unaffected. Waivers come with limits on time and tasks and reassessment at least every three years, or sooner if circumstances change.

These rules protect the public and follow from the nature of aviation work and the need to keep physical fitness during duty. They set requirements for people in this occupation and are not punitive, so they fit the earlier principles and do not conflict with the right to work.

who: Aviation personnel granted physical defect waivers
Civil aviation authority and aviation medical examiners

raw.answer: The case asked whether prison sentences for people who use drugs, under two older drug-control laws, violate the Constitution. The court held that these provisions do not conflict with Articles 8 and 23 of the Constitution, because their aim is to deter drug use through the general preventive effect of punishment. It also noted that later amendments fit these principles better, and said the rule leaving already-sentenced cases under the old law should be reviewed.
raw.held: The prison and fine penalties for drug use in the Eradication of Narcotics Ordinance (Article 9, paragraph 1) and the Narcotics Drugs Control Act (Article 13-1, paragraph 2, item 4) do not conflict with Constitution Articles 8 and 23. The legislature is urged to review excluding finally sentenced or ongoing cases from the new system.

points.text: Punishment is a last-resort coercive measure, but the legislature is free to choose how to punish anti-social conduct. Special criminal laws are consistent with proportionality if they meet legitimate purpose, necessity and appropriateness of restriction under Article 23, as in Interpretation No. 476.

Prison sentences seriously restrict personal freedom, so they are justified only where forced isolation and treatment is needed to protect social order, and the penalty must reflect how harmful the conduct is and how important the protected interest is.

Drug use may be seen as self-harm, but it damages the nervous system, creates dependence, ruins individuals and families, can link to serious crimes and worsens public safety, so the legislature may regulate it with punishment at the stage of abstract danger.

The old provisions did not distinguish addicted from non-addicted users or fully weigh the degree of harm, but their purpose was to use the general deterrent effect of punishment to discourage drug use, which matches the principles above, so they do not conflict with Articles 8 and 23.

Later amendments graded drugs by harm, distinguished first, repeat and later offenders, added treatment and supervision measures, and replaced punishment with security measures for first and repeat offenders without continued drug-use tendency, which better fits these principles.

Article 35, item 4 of the new act leaves finally sentenced or ongoing cases under the old rules. This is not inconsistent with Article 2, paragraph 3 of the Criminal Code, but it should be reviewed to deepen the new criminal policy.

who: People already sentenced or serving sentences under the old laws

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Judicial Yuan rule that ends the fixed term of judges who also serve as division chiefs (庭長) in the courts below the top level, and removes them from that administrative post, violates the Constitution. The court decided it does not. Ending the division-chief post only changes an administrative duty and leaves the person's status as a judge intact. The court also said it would be better for the selection and removal of division chiefs to be set by statute.
raw.held: The rule that removes a judge from the division-chief post when the term ends does not conflict with Article 81's protection of judges' status, because it is only an administrative adjustment. The court also pointed out that it is preferable for a law to govern how division chiefs are selected and removed.

points.text: Article 80 requires judicial independence. Article 81 protects judges' status. Personnel actions that affect a judge's status and rights need a legal basis, but actions that do not touch them may be reasonable judicial administration if they do not breach independence.

A division chief supervises only the auxiliary administrative work needed for trials. A presiding judge is a separate role, set up to direct proceedings. In deciding cases, the presiding judge has the same powers as the other judges on the panel.
Article 81 therefore protects judges who conduct independent trials, not the administrative post of division chief.

A judge who is also a division chief has more duties and a higher starting pay grade, but the highest grade reachable as a judge is the same. Their legal rights and interests are no different, so dropping the post is not a demotion.

Ending the division-chief post removes only the administrative role. It does not harm the person's work as a judge or their existing rank, grade or pay, so it is just an adjustment of agency administration. The judicial administration authority acted within its organizational powers.

A sound system around trials supports fair and effective adjudication, and division chiefs help with that. To uphold Article 82's requirement that court organization be set by law, the court said choosing and removing division chiefs is best handled by an overall plan set out in law.

who: Judges who also serve as division chiefs
Judicial Yuan and judicial administration authorities

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Organized Crime Prevention Act's rule requiring forced labor after a prison sentence for organized crime is unconstitutional. The court decided it is not, because it serves a needed purpose and the law lets prosecutors and courts waive or end the forced labor in individual cases.
raw.held: Article 3, paragraph 3 of the Organized Crime Prevention Act, which orders forced labor of three or five years after the sentence is served or pardoned, does not conflict with Article 8 (personal freedom) or Article 23 (proportionality) of the Constitution.

points.text: Forced labor as a security measure aims to build work habits and skills so people can support themselves after returning to society, serving the criminal law's goal of reform.

The Act targets organized groups of three or more with internal structure and a criminal purpose, which differs from the earlier gun-control provision (Interpretation No. 471) that ordered forced labor regardless of a person's criminal habits or need for correction.
Organized crime is hierarchical, tightly controlled and habitual, and harms society and threatens democracy far more than ordinary non-organized crime.
The forced labor rule supplements the shortcomings of punishment and helps reintegration, and it helps deter organized crime, so it is necessary to protect social order and people's rights.

Paragraphs 4 and 5 allow the prosecutor to seek waiver, or an early end, of forced labor where it is unnecessary, so courts can weigh each person's circumstances and human-rights principles in a suitable, necessary and reasonable way.

who: People convicted under the Organized Crime Prevention Act

raw.answer: The case asked whether an older interpretation (院字第2810號), which said an appeal is pointless when the harm can no longer be remedied, wrongly shuts out appeals once an election is over. The court said that interpretation does not cover rights that can be exercised again and again, such as running in elections. So a person rejected as a candidate can still have the case heard even after that election has ended, as long as that type of election continues to exist.
raw.held: The court supplemented the earlier interpretation: when a person's application to run for public office is rejected and the election has since finished, the courts must still accept the case, because the right to stand for election is protected by the constitution and can be exercised repeatedly, so the case still has a point if that election system continues.

points.text: People have constitutional rights to take examinations and to hold public office, including offices filled by election, and if they claim these rights were violated they should be allowed to bring a case in court.
The earlier interpretation means a case needs a real need for legal protection, so it is pointless only when no review could fix the harm or restore the person's position.
That 'cannot be remedied' idea does not include rights that by the design of the state system recur and can be used repeatedly, such as taking part in elections or examinations.
Even if time has passed and the earlier situation cannot be restored, a case still has a point where similar situations can reasonably be expected to happen again.

A rejected candidate applicant's right to run is protected and repeatable, so unless that election no longer exists, the outcome still matters for later elections. The agency or court must still examine the case on its merits, and if the rejection was unlawful or improper it should cancel it so the person is not rejected again in similar elections.

The challenge to two other rules (article 35 of the election and recall law and article 13 of the Executive Yuan's appeals committee rules) was not accepted, because they were not applied in the final court decision.

who: People rejected as candidates for public office
People taking examinations or seeking public service

raw.answer: The case asked whether government letters treating men born in 1975 (year 64 of the Republic) as the first group to be drafted in Kinmen and Matsu were unconstitutional. Earlier rules had let some young men there be certified as trained reserve-status militia, and those rules ended when wartime administration ended. The court held that the letters cannot be applied to the extent they drafted men born in 1975 without checking whether they met the certification requirements.
raw.held: The parts of the three government letters that made all men born in 1975 the first draft group in Kinmen and Matsu, regardless of whether they met the certification requirements, must not be applied. When ending the old rules, the authorities should have provided reasonable remedies or a transition period.

points.text: When an agency amends or repeals a regulation, it must consider the protection of the trust people placed in it. If people's concrete legal benefits are harmed, it should provide reasonable remedies or a transition period.
This protection also covers people who relied on a legal position obtained under mandatory rules before the repeal or amendment.
Wartime administration in Kinmen and Matsu ended, the certification measures were repealed, and the area returned to the normal conscription system.

Men who already met the measures' requirements could have been certified, but those who had not yet applied lost that legal position when the measures were repealed, so their trust should be protected.
Making men born in 1975 the first draft group affected their service category, training period, call-up duties and whether they could be called to combat, so a remedy or transition period was needed.

The letters, which drafted men born in 1975 whether or not they met the requirements, therefore cannot be applied on the basis of trust protection. Whether the petitioners' own cases meet the requirements is for the authorities to judge from all the evidence.

who: Men in Kinmen and Matsu born in 1975
Men in Kinmen and Matsu who had not yet applied for certification

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 177 of the 1988 Securities and Exchange Act was unconstitutional. Item 3 of that article punished anyone who broke other prohibition, suspension or restriction orders issued by the authority under the Act, but left what counted as a punishable act to administrative orders. The court held that this did not meet the constitutional requirement of clarity in criminal punishment, so the provision must stop being applied.
raw.held: Article 177, item 3 of the Securities and Exchange Act as amended on 29 January 1988 is inconsistent with the Constitution's protection of people's rights, and it must stop being applied from the day the interpretation was announced.

points.text: The legislature may authorize administrative agencies to issue supplementary orders, but the purpose, content and scope of the authorization must be specific and clear, and the clarity required should match the orders' effect on people's rights.

Criminal law affects life, liberty and property so greatly that it must be set by statute. If a law lets an agency fill in details, people must be able to foresee from the law itself which conduct is punishable.

Punishing securities officers and staff for breaking business prohibition, suspension or restriction orders limits people's rights, so the types of punishable conduct should be stated in the Securities and Exchange Act itself.

Item 3 left the content of punishable conduct to administrative orders, so it could only be known by reading those orders. This is unclear authorization and conflicts with the constitutional protection of rights.
Conduct that was unlawful under the law at the time cannot be defended or relieved by relying on this interpretation.
The provision was deleted in July 2000. The court suggested reviewing which violations of such orders that harm securities market order should be punishable, and setting suitable rules.

who: People facing criminal penalties under the Act

raw.answer: The case asked whether the rules on counting past service and setting rank and grade when staff move between administrative, educational and public-enterprise jobs are unconstitutional. The court found the transfer measures were within what the law authorized and did not violate Article 7 of the Constitution. But it said one rule, which caps counted service at the top of the basic pay scale, is inconsistent with later rules and should be reviewed and improved.
raw.held: The transfer measures (Article 7 of the transfer measures and Article 15, paragraph 3 of the 1987 enforcement rules) were held not unconstitutional. The cap on counted service at the highest basic pay level does not match later rules, which allow it up to the highest merit pay level, and should be reviewed and improved.

points.text: The transfer measures were made under Article 16 of the Civil Service Appointment Act, which authorizes rules for counting past service when staff move between the three types of jobs, so people with the same basic qualifications can exchange and fill middle and senior posts.
Article 7 of the measures is needed to set the standard for counting service and setting rank and grade, so it fits what the law authorized.

The 1987 enforcement rule capping yearly pay-step additions at the top basic pay step reflects that the three systems have different appointment, pay and evaluation rules, so staff cannot simply be moved over at their old pay level. It was designed for fairness within the personnel system.
For these reasons the rules did not violate Article 16 of the Civil Service Pay Act, Article 11 of the Central Regulations Standard Act, or Article 7 of the Constitution.

However, the measures' cap at the top basic pay step is inconsistent with the enforcement rules revised from December 26, 1995 onward, which allow additions up to the top merit pay step, so it should be reviewed and improved.

who: Administrative, education and public-enterprise staff who transfer between systems
Civil servants whose past service is counted for rank and pay
Examination authorities and personnel agencies who set the rules

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Civil Code's age rules for adoption are unconstitutional. The rules say the adopter must be at least 20 years older than the adoptee, and an adoption that breaks this rule is void. The court held that the rules do not violate the Constitution, but said the relevant authorities should review them and add flexibility for couples adopting together and for a spouse adopting the other spouse's child.
raw.held: The 20-year age-gap rule (Article 1073) and the rule that adoptions breaking it are void (Article 1079-1) do not conflict with the Constitution's protection of people's freedoms and rights. The court also said the rule should be made flexible for joint adoption by a couple or adoption of a spouse's child, and the authorities should review and amend it.

points.text: The age-gap and voidness rules respect the tradition of generations and fit Taiwan's ideas of family ethics.
The rules are necessary to maintain social order and advance the public interest, so they do not conflict with the Constitution's protection of freedoms and rights.
What counts as a reasonable age gap between adopter and adoptee is a matter for the legislature's discretion.
Adoption law aims to protect the adopted child, and family relationships in society are growing more complex.
When a couple adopts together or a spouse adopts the other's child, failing the age rule makes the adoption void, which can harm the adoptee and family happiness.
To support family harmony and the adopted child's rights, the rule should be flexible in those cases to meet real social needs, and the authorities should review and amend it.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a tax rule and a Ministry of Finance letter about taxing shares a company issues out of its undistributed earnings (bonus shares) were unconstitutional. The court decided that both are consistent with the Constitution. It found that the rule stays within what the Income Tax Act authorizes and that the letter is a necessary interpretation of the tax laws.
raw.held: Article 70, paragraph 1 of the Enforcement Rules of the Income Tax Act does not go beyond the authority the Income Tax Act gives it and does not violate the Constitution. The Ministry of Finance's 1975 letter is a proper interpretation, consistent with the purpose of the Statute for Upgrading Industries, and does not conflict with the principle of taxation by law in Article 19 of the Constitution.

points.text: Income tax on businesses is broadly defined: all business and other income is taxable unless the law grants a specific exemption, which serves fair sharing of the tax burden.

Laws may authorize agencies to make necessary rules by clear and specific authorization. Whether a rule fits the authorization is judged by the law's purpose and overall structure, not just its wording.
