Tax authorities may issue necessary interpretations in line with a law's purpose, the economic function of the tax, and fairness in taxing, as earlier interpretations Nos. 420 and 438 stated.

The Income Tax Act's Article 76-1 sets out how undistributed earnings are treated, whether they are used to increase capital or not. The rule on taxing shares issued from such earnings does not exceed the purpose and scope of that article and related provisions.

The Ministry's letter only explains that shares received through reinvestment may be exempt from the year's taxable income but must still be counted in the company's total income. This prevents business or other income from falling outside taxation, and it matches the purpose of the investment-encouragement law.
Therefore both the rule and the letter do not conflict with Article 19 of the Constitution.

raw.answer: The case asked how the President of the Judicial Yuan, the Vice President, and the Grand Justices should be appointed if seats became vacant before the sixth-term Grand Justices' terms ended in 2003. The constitutional amendments did not say. The court decided that the President nominates and the Legislative Yuan must consent.
raw.held: Until the sixth-term Grand Justices' terms end in 2003, vacancies among the Grand Justices and the Judicial Yuan's President and Vice President are to be filled by Presidential nomination with the Legislative Yuan's consent.

points.text: The current amendments say nothing about how vacancies are filled before 2003, yet these offices are part of the constitutional system and have set powers, so their appointment cannot be left without a rule. The court must fill this gap in line with the constitution as a whole.

Across the constitution and its amendments, the President nominates and appoints, while consent comes from a body with a popular mandate. The consent body was first the Control Yuan, then the National Assembly.

The 2000 amendments reduced the National Assembly's role and moved consent for Judicial, Examination and Control Yuan appointments to the Legislative Yuan, so the National Assembly can no longer consent to these appointments.

Democratic government needs a popular basis to be legitimate, so the Legislative Yuan, as the representative body, must give consent. Consequently, when a vacancy affects the Judicial Yuan's normal operation, the President nominates and the Legislative Yuan consents.

who: Grand Justices and Judicial Yuan leaders

raw.answer: This ruling (Interpretation No. 527) deals with how local self-governing bodies in Taiwan set up their offices and positions, and who may ask the Constitutional Court for an interpretation when disputes arise under the Local Government Act. The court explained that offices must generally be created through an organizational self-government ordinance, and it set out which bodies may apply for an interpretation and by what route in disputes with higher authorities.
raw.held: Local bodies must create offices and positions under an organizational ordinance, with a limited temporary exception where a law clearly requires a position. The court also set out who may apply for an interpretation, and how, in disputes over resolutions, local rules and supervisory actions, and said pure disputes over authority must follow the procedure in Article 77 of the Act.

points.text: Local self-governing bodies have the power to organize themselves and to make and carry out rules on their own affairs, within the Constitution and the law. Offices and positions must be set up by the local legislature through an organizational ordinance based on the central authority's standards.

Where a law clearly requires a position and making the rules will take time, the local executive may set it up first and appoint staff as a temporary measure for real operational needs. Positions the law merely allows need an ordinance as their basis.

The Act's provisions on asking for an interpretation apply when a supervising authority doubts that a resolution or local rule conflicts with higher law but has not declared it void. If the local body disagrees with a notice declaring something void, its legislature (for an ordinance) or its executive (for an administrative rule) may apply, without the forwarding step of Article 9, because the higher authority is a party to the dispute.

Local executives cannot go straight to the court over disputes with their own legislature on carrying out resolutions, and a legislature cannot pass a resolution and then seek an interpretation that it conflicts with higher law. The Act has no provision letting some members apply, and doing so would breach the principle against contradicting oneself.

A local body may apply directly under Article 75, paragraph 8 only if the supervisor's action involves the validity of a local rule said to violate higher norms and that rule has not been declared void. The court reviews norms, not individual administrative acts, so other harm must go through administrative lawsuits and, after all appeals, possibly an application; pure authority disputes follow Article 77.

For other applications, a local legislature may apply by resolution without forwarding. A local government may apply directly on its own affairs where it is not bound by the central authority's views, but for centrally commissioned matters the Article 9 procedure still applies.

raw.answer: The case asked whether the government must first change the urban plan before it expropriates private land in an urban planning area that is not designated for public facilities. The court said yes: it must go through the procedure to change the urban plan first, and only then expropriate. It also ruled on how the 30-day public notice period works for expropriation under the Land Act.
raw.held: When the government needs to expropriate private land in an urban planning area that was not public-facility land in order to build public facilities, it must first change the urban plan and then expropriate. Expropriating without doing so violates Article 52 of the Urban Planning Act. An expropriation without lawful public notice, or without the 30-day period, has no effect, and if the notice date is wrong the actual notice date counts.

points.text: An urban plan takes binding effect once announced and finalized, so government use or expropriation of land must conform to it, and because expropriation takes away property rights, the legal requirements and procedures must be strictly followed.

Article 52 (first part) of the Urban Planning Act bars expropriation of private land from hampering the local urban plan, so the government must carefully examine whether the project is necessary and whether it hampers the plan.
So, unless a law provides otherwise, the urban plan must be changed before non-public-facility private land is expropriated; expropriating without that change violates the rule.
Such an expropriation is a flawed administrative act, but how it can be challenged is a separate question the ruling does not address.
Under the Land Act, expropriation without lawful public notice, or without observing the 30-day period, has no effect.
If the date written in the notice differs from the actual notice date, the actual date controls, and the expropriation takes effect when 30 days from the actual notice have passed.

who: Owners of private land in urban planning areas

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Criminal Code's defamation offence violates the constitution's protection of free speech. The court decided it does not: the defamation provisions are a permitted limit on speech, and the clause excusing true statements must be read so speakers are not forced to prove truth themselves.
raw.held: Criminal defamation under Article 310, paragraphs 1 and 2, is consistent with the constitution. Article 310, paragraph 3 is also consistent, provided it is read so that a speaker who cannot prove truth but had reasonable grounds to believe it true is not punished, and prosecutors or private complainants still must prove intent to harm reputation.

points.text: Free speech is a basic right that the state should protect as fully as possible, because it serves self-expression, exchange of views, the search for truth and oversight of political and social activity.
The law may still reasonably limit speech, depending on how it is spread, to protect personal reputation, privacy and the public interest.

Whether to use civil compensation alone or also criminal punishment depends on several factors; on Taiwan's present situation, not decriminalizing defamation is not unconstitutional, and money-only liability would let wealthy people defame others freely.

Paragraphs 1 and 2 set different penalties for spoken defamation and for defamation by writing or pictures; they are necessary to prevent harm to others' rights and meet the proportionality principle in Article 23.

The exemption for provably true statements protects speech that matches the facts; it does not require the speaker to prove truth personally. A speaker with reasonable grounds to believe the statement true, based on the evidence offered, cannot be punished for defamation.

Prosecutors or private complainants still bear the burden of proving intent to damage reputation, and courts still have a duty to find out whether the statement is true. Article 311's good-faith exemptions protect honest expression and raise no constitutional problem.

who: People who make statements about others

raw.answer: The case asked whether it is unconstitutional to punish reserve soldiers who move without reporting it, and to punish more heavily when the move means a call-up order cannot be delivered. The court found these rules do not violate the Constitution. It said the reporting duty does not restrict freedom of residence and that the punishments are within the legislature's lawmaking discretion.
raw.held: The criminal penalty for reserve soldiers who move without a valid reason and fail to report it does not violate Article 10 of the Constitution. The heavier punishment when a call-up order cannot be delivered, which treats the act as intent to avoid call-up, does not violate Article 23 either. Rules on fault (責任要件) still apply.

points.text: The Constitution sets a duty to serve in the military but does not say how conscription and call-ups work, so the legislature decides by law, weighing national security and social development, including the penalties for breaching the duty.

Whether to punish a breach of administrative duties with an administrative fine or a criminal penalty is for the legislature to decide, and it is not unconstitutional unless it exceeds proportionality. A different law using a fine for a different purpose does not bar criminal penalties elsewhere.

Reserve soldiers living somewhere other than their registered address affects public interests under the military service laws, so the legislature could use a criminal penalty to control reservist movements and keep the call-up system working. Courts can still set a suitable sentence within the legal range, so the law is not excessively harsh and fits proportionality.

Failing to report a move that leads to undeliverable call-up orders has already harmed call-ups and seriously affected national security, so treating it as intent to avoid call-up is within the legislature's discretion.
The reporting rule only requires reservists to notify authorities of a move so orders can be delivered, and it does not limit freedom to choose or change residence.
Treating undeliverable orders as intent to avoid call-up does not remove the requirement of fault, which still applies.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Civil Service letter was unconstitutional for refusing retirement compensation for service before the Council for Economic Planning and Development was restructured in 1985. The Court decided the letter was not unconstitutional. Only service from the restructuring until June 30, 1995 qualifies for compensation under the 1995 measures.
raw.held: The Court held that the Ministry's letter, which pays compensation only for service from the January 9, 1985 restructuring through June 30, 1995 and not for earlier service, fits the purpose of the compensation measures and does not conflict with the constitutional protection of property rights.

points.text: The 1995 compensation measures were a policy-based remedy for ordinary public school and government employees, whose early retirement pay calculations left out 'other cash benefits'.
The Constitution's equality guarantee is substantive, not mechanical, so reasonable differences in treatment are allowed when the nature of the matter differs.
Staff of the Council before restructuring had a different hiring process and pay system from ordinary civil servants, and under a single salary scheme had no 'other cash benefits' component.

Their pre-restructuring service had already been settled through a difference payment, and the retirement pay per base unit was higher than for ordinary civil servants. For overall balance among public employees, the measures therefore do not cover that service.
The Ministry's letter was a necessary supplementary rule issued within its authority to carry out unclear measures, consistent with their original intent and not in conflict with property rights.

who: Former staff of the Council for Economic Planning and Development
Ordinary public school and government employees

raw.answer: The case asked which court, administrative or ordinary, should handle a government request to take back public housing and enforce that order under the National Housing Act. The court decided it is a civil matter for the ordinary courts, so a civil division cannot reject the request just because administrative courts now exist.
raw.held: Contracts of sale, lease or loan made by the housing authority are private-law relations, so taking back housing under Article 21(1) is a civil matter for the ordinary courts. An administrative court that lacks jurisdiction must dismiss the case and transfer it to the ordinary court, which must resume hearing it.

points.text: The state may pursue its tasks through public-law or private-law acts. Disputes go to administrative courts if public-law and to ordinary courts if private-law, though the legislature may set a different arrangement, which then binds all organs and courts.

Apart from privately built housing, the authority approves an applicant and then signs a sale, lease or loan contract. These are private-economy measures for social welfare with no power-subordination relationship, so they are not an exercise of public power.

The provision letting the authority take back housing and seek court enforcement gives enforceability to specific breaches of contract. It concerns private rights, so the court named is the ordinary court.

Earlier cases that were really public-law matters went through civil litigation only because administrative litigation lacked suitable procedures, but this housing matter is private-law and so differs.

The court's finding on jurisdiction in this case is treated as settled and binds all courts. An earlier ordinary-court dismissal for lack of jurisdiction was a flawed decision and has no binding force.

The administrative court must dismiss and transfer the case, and the receiving court must restore it and hear it, in order to protect the constitutional right to sue. The relevant authorities are told to review and design a way to resolve such jurisdiction conflicts.

who: Buyers, tenants and borrowers of public housing

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance directive was unconstitutional. The directive treats only half of the compensation paid to a tenant farmer, when the government expropriates rented farmland, as that year's income, and leaves the other half untaxed. The court held that the directive does not violate the Constitution.
raw.held: The directive counting half of a tenant farmer's expropriation compensation as income for the year, with the other half tax-free, is consistent with the income tax law and does not conflict with Constitution Articles 15, 19 and 23. It also does not violate the equal-treatment principle in Article 7 by being treated differently from the 1977 directive on crop compensation in land sales.

points.text: Compensation a tenant farmer receives when the lease ends under the law counts as income from Taiwan sources and is not tax-exempt. It is therefore taxable as 'other income' under the income tax law.

The compensation builds up over many years, and income tax rates rise with income. Taxing it all in one year would increase the tenant's tax burden. Counting only half is allowed for the comparable compensation paid when a landlord takes back land.

Compensation from expropriation is similar in nature to that landlord-recovery compensation. So the directive's half-income treatment is fair, lightens the tenant's burden and fits the income tax provisions.
For these reasons the directive does not conflict with the protection of property (Art. 15), taxation according to law (Art. 19) or the legal-reservation principle (Art. 23).

The other directive, on crop compensation in land sales, deals with a loss compensation, while the expropriation directive deals with other income. Their natures differ, so they cannot be compared and equal treatment is not violated.

who: Tenant farmers on expropriated rented farmland
Landowners whose rented farmland is expropriated

raw.answer: The case asked whether a 1995 Ministry of Civil Service letter was unconstitutional. It ended a rule that let reserve officers who served four years be ranked and paid at an equivalent grade when moving into public jobs. The court held the letter was not unconstitutional, even though having no transition period was open to criticism.
raw.held: The 1995 letter that stopped applying the ranking preference for reserve officers moving into public service is consistent with the governing statute and does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: Protection of reasonable reliance is a constitutional principle. It covers the repeal or change of administrative rules, not only the withdrawal of benefits granted by individual administrative decisions.

An agency may repeal or change a rule for the public interest. If people who relied on the old rule would lose substantive benefits and no existing remedy applies, the agency should offer reasonable relief or a transition period.

Reliance gets no protection if the rule seriously and obviously violates a higher norm, if it was issued because of improper means or false information, or if it is only a hope or expectation with no concrete sign of reliance.

Protecting the open competitive examination system and the regular civil-service recruitment channel outweighs a special preference for the few officers who served longer. So stopping the rule served the public interest, though the lack of a transition period was open to criticism.
The 1987 letter could serve as a basis for reliance. But it was a stopgap for recruiting soldiers and did not match the statute, so no one could expect it to last forever.

Reliance needs concrete conduct, such as taking the exam or qualifying to apply for ranking. The petitioner had not passed the exam or obtained qualification when the rule stopped, having passed only in 1997, so he could not claim reliance protection.

who: Reserve officers who served four years of active duty
Applicants for public-service exams and ranking
The Ministry of Civil Service and rule-making agencies

raw.answer: The case asked whether a 1987 Ministry of Finance directive was unconstitutional. It said that businesses in bonded zones (such as export processing zones, science parks, and bonded factories or warehouses) that sell goods into the domestic taxable area without customs declaration must issue a uniform invoice and pay business tax. The court decided the directive is not unconstitutional.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance directive is a technical supplementary rule that fits the Business Tax Act's purpose. It does not violate the principle that taxes must be set by law, and it does not conflict with Article 19 of the Constitution or the cited Business Tax Act provisions.

points.text: Taxes must have a legal basis, but laws cannot cover every detail, so administrative orders may address technical and detailed tax matters within the limits of the law's purpose.
Goods entering bonded zones are not treated as imports and are exempt from tax only because they stay in the zone and are processed and then re-exported.
When such goods are sold into the domestic area they are still untaxed bonded goods and must be declared to customs, which counts as an import under Article 5, item 2, with tax paid.

Goods that need no customs declaration fall outside that import definition and are like ordinary domestic sales, so a uniform invoice and business tax are required. This differs from the import exemption in Article 41, paragraph 2.

The directive was issued under the ministry's legal authority to carry out the Business Tax Act and prevent tax evasion, so it is a technical supplement that fits the Act and does not breach the principle of taxation by law.

The Science Park Administration's letter about issuing receipts was only an internal management notice. That body is not a tax authority and cannot interpret or change tax law, so it does not compete with the ministry's directive.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a provision of the Anti-Narcotics Act that stops defendants from appealing to the third-instance Supreme Court is unconstitutional. The court decided it is not. It found the limit to be a reasonable special procedure that does not violate the right to bring lawsuits, equality, or the proportionality principle.
raw.held: Article 16 (first part) of the Act, which makes the high court the final court for drug offenses and limits appeals to the Supreme Court in cases of imprisonment or lighter sentences, is a reasonable restriction. It does not violate Articles 16, 7 or 23 of the Constitution.

points.text: The constitutional right to sue protects the right to proper legal procedures and a fair trial. The legislature decides, by law and in a reasonable way, which court levels, procedures and requirements apply.

The legislature saw drugs as very harmful to society and the offenses as needing security measures. It set up a special procedure to strengthen deterrence and protect public health, which is a reasonable limit.

Appeals to the third-instance court may be made only on grounds of violation of law, and a final judgment that violates the law can be remedied through extraordinary appeal under Articles 377 and 441 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. So a remedy exists for second-instance judgments of imprisonment or lighter.

Death and life-imprisonment cases are sent to the Supreme Court for review automatically, which takes the defendant's interests into account and stays within the legislature's freedom to design the system.
The Act still gives defendants the right to appeal to the second instance, so their right to sue is not taken away. The rule does not breach the proportionality principle (Article 23) or Article 7.

who: Defendants charged under the anti-narcotics law
People sentenced to imprisonment or less for drug offenses
Defendants facing death or life imprisonment in drug cases
